analysis: Antoine-Louis Barye at $1,000-1,500 with eight photographs -- the best-documented bronze in Day 3. Barye is the founding figure of the French animalier school and a period Barye is a genuinely important object.
problems: Out of band, just. Barye is also the most recast sculptor in the category: after his death the Brame and Barbedienne editions ran for decades, and 20th-century copies are endless. Eight photographs make this the one bronze in the run where the chasing quality can actually be judged before preview -- use them.
patience: Not applicable -- out of band. Recasts are everywhere; period casts are not.

analysis: The second Barye at $1,000-2,000.
problems: Out of band. Same recasting caveats. Two Baryes in one sale means the room's animalier money will split.

analysis: Joseph Heinrichs (1866-1937) at $1,000-1,500. Heinrichs made Arts and Crafts copper and silver-mounted hollowware in New York -- hammered copper with silver rims, often in the Nouveau taste.
problems: Out of band, just. This is metalware rather than a painting despite where it sits in the catalogue. Establish what the piece is; his coffee sets and jardinieres differ a lot in value. Note the brief's caution that decorative copper is a weak market.

analysis: Francois Leon Sicard (France, 1862-1934) at $3,000-5,000. Sicard is best known for the Archibald Fountain in Sydney; a substantial academic sculptor.
problems: Far out of band. Same period-versus-later-cast question as every bronze in this run.

analysis: S.C. Yuan (CA, 1911-1974) at $6,000-8,000. Yuan was a Monterey painter whose reputation and prices have risen sharply in recent years.
problems: Far out of band and wrong coast.

analysis: Bessie Potter Vonnoh (1872-1955) at $3,000-5,000. Vonnoh was among the most successful American women sculptors of her generation, known for intimate domestic bronzes, and her market has strengthened with the reassessment of women artists.
problems: Far out of band. Her small bronzes were cast in editions during her lifetime, so establish the foundry and edition.

analysis: Aldro T. Hibbard (MA/VT, 1886-1972) at $6,000-8,000. Hibbard was the leading painter of New England winter landscapes and a founder of the Rockport art colony.
problems: Far out of band. His snow scenes are the sought-after subject; five photographs.

analysis: Chester Beach (1881-1956) at $1,000-1,500. A significant American sculptor of the early 20th century with work in the Metropolitan.
problems: Out of band, just. Note the catalogue punctuates the entry as 'ITALY. 1881-1956' with a stray period. Establish whether bronze or marble and whether a lifetime cast.

analysis: Russell Wray at $4,000-6,000 -- the dearest of three Wray lots (3085, 3087, 3089). Note the catalogue gives his state as NY here and CA on the other two, which is inconsistent within the same sale.
problems: Far out of band, living artist, and only two photographs for a four-figure lot. The state inconsistency is another small cataloguing failure.

analysis: Second Russell Wray at $1,500-2,000.
problems: Out of band, living artist.

analysis: Third and cheapest Russell Wray at $1,200-1,600.
problems: Out of band, living artist, three lots in the sale.

analysis: Gretna Campbell (NY, 1922-1987) at $3,000-5,000. Campbell painted on Great Cranberry Island, Maine for decades and is a genuinely respected second-generation New York School landscape painter with a rising reputation.
problems: Far out of band. Worth knowing about because her Maine connection is real and her market is moving upward -- if a smaller Campbell appeared at a Maine sale in band it would be worth pursuing.

analysis: Ronald Goldfinger (CA, 1946-2021) at $2,000-3,000.
problems: Out of band, wrong coast, thin record.

analysis: Jack Cassinetto (CA, 1944-2018) at $2,000-3,000, with a second at 3174 for $1,500-2,000. A California painter of rural barns and still lifes.
problems: Out of band and wrong coast. Two lots in the sale.

analysis: The second Jack Cassinetto at $1,500-2,000.
problems: Out of band, wrong coast.

analysis: Hugo Robus at $2,000-3,000 -- the major Robus of the two, against 3110 at $600-800 which I have rated BUY IF CHEAP. Robus was a significant American modernist sculptor.
problems: Out of band. 3110 is the accessible one.

analysis: Moses Soyer (1899-1974) at $2,000-3,000 -- brother of Raphael Soyer, whose work appears at 1083 in Day 1. Both were leading Social Realists.
problems: Out of band. The two Soyer lots across the sale suggest a related consignment; 1083 at $600-800 is the affordable one.

analysis: Stan Phillips (NY/MA, 1923-2012) at $2,000-3,000.
problems: Out of band, thin record.

analysis: Daniel Chester French (1850-1931) at $2,500-3,500. French is one of the most important American sculptors there has been -- the Lincoln Memorial and the Minute Man at Concord.
problems: Far out of band. At this estimate it will be a reduction, a posthumous cast or a studio piece rather than an autograph work. French's popular compositions were editioned in bronze reductions for decades. Establish the foundry mark and whether it is a lifetime cast.

analysis: Charles Shepard Chapman (NY/NJ, 1879-1962) at $2,000-3,000. A National Academician and illustrator-turned-landscape painter.
problems: Out of band.

analysis: Stephan Abel Sinding (1846-1922) at $2,000-3,000. A Norwegian-Danish sculptor of real standing; died in 1922, so unambiguously antique.
problems: Out of band. Same lifetime-versus-later-cast question. Five photographs.

analysis: Chester Coleman Hayes (NY/France, 1867-1947) at $2,000-3,000.
problems: Out of band. Minor name with a thin record for the estimate.

analysis: Clara Cohan (NY/AZ/ME, 1956- ) at $2,000-3,000. A Maine association is listed among three states.
problems: Out of band, living artist, and the Maine claim is one of three. Three photographs.

analysis: Barbara Kassel (NY, 1952- ) at $1,200-1,500.
problems: Out of band, living artist.

analysis: Louis Marie Moret (France, 1818-1883) at $2,000-3,000. Died in 1883, so unambiguously antique.
problems: Out of band. Minor French name; five photographs.

analysis: Harold C. Wolcott at $2,000-3,000, the middle of three Wolcott lots.
problems: Out of band. 3164 at $800-1,200 is the accessible one.

analysis: The dearest Harold Wolcott at $3,000-4,000.
problems: Out of band. A steep estimate for an artist with a thin public record.

analysis: Laura D. Stroud Ladd (PA, 1864-1943) at $1,500-2,000 with five photographs. Career begins well before 1926.
problems: Out of band. Minor name.

analysis: Bernard Corey (MA, 1914-2000) at $1,000-1,500. A New England landscape painter with a steady regional market.
problems: Out of band, just. Corey was prolific and his work appears frequently in New England sales.

analysis: Elizabeth Curtis (NY, 1873-1946) at $1,000-1,500. Career begins well before 1926.
problems: Out of band, just. Minor name.

analysis: Jane Peterson (1876-1965) at $5,000-7,500. Peterson was a genuinely accomplished American modernist whose flower pieces and Gloucester harbour scenes have a strong market, and her reputation has risen considerably.
problems: Far out of band. Three photographs. Peterson is also faked, and her bold gouaches are easier to imitate than her oils.

analysis: Three Karl Springer stone candle holders at $2,000-3,000. Springer was a leading 1970s and 80s American designer whose lacquer and exotic-material furniture has a strong collector market.
problems: Out of band. Only two photographs for a three-piece lot. Springer is also widely attributed to without documentation -- 'Springer style' is a common trade description.

analysis: Avinash Chandra (UK/India, 1931-1991) at $3,000-5,000, one of two. Chandra was the first Indian artist to exhibit widely in Britain and his market has strengthened with the growth in South Asian modernism.
problems: Far out of band. That market is in London and Mumbai rather than New England.

analysis: The second Avinash Chandra at $3,000-5,000.
problems: Far out of band.

analysis: John Rudge (NY/Italy/UK, 1925-1971) at $1,000-1,500, one of two.
problems: Out of band, just. Thin record.

analysis: The second John Rudge at $1,000-1,500.
problems: Out of band.

analysis: Clyde Butcher (FL, 1942- ) at $3,000-4,000. Butcher is the leading large-format black-and-white photographer of the Florida Everglades, often compared to Ansel Adams.
problems: Far out of band. Photography also depends heavily on print size, date and edition -- five photographs but none of that is stated.

analysis: Robert Motherwell at $2,500-3,500. Note the catalogue calls him 'Robert Burns Motherwell', which is correct -- his full name -- though rarely used.
problems: Far out of band. At this price it is a print rather than a painting; Motherwell's editioned lithographs and aquatints are common and his paintings are seven figures. Establish edition and signature.

analysis: Margaret 'Meta' Kilgallen (CA, 1967-2001) at $8,000-12,000. Kilgallen was a central figure in the Mission School and her early death has made her work scarce and sought after.
problems: Far out of band. Only two photographs for a five-figure lot, which for an artist whose market depends heavily on provenance and authentication is inadequate.

analysis: Joy Laville (UK/Mexico, 1923- ) at $8,000-12,000. A significant figure in Mexican modern art with a strong domestic market.
problems: Far out of band. That market is in Mexico City.

analysis: Attributed to Louise Nevelson at $2,000-3,000. Nevelson's black assemblage constructions are major American sculpture.
problems: Out of band, and 'attributed to' per the standing principles. Nevelson's estate and authentication are also contested territory. A genuine Nevelson is worth many multiples of this, so the estimate itself signals the house's confidence level.

analysis: Leo Villareal (NY, 1967- ) at $40,000-60,000 -- the most expensive lot in the entire sale. Villareal makes LED light sculptures and did the Bay Lights installation on the Bay Bridge.
problems: Forty to sixty times the ceiling. Also worth noting practically: an LED light work is an electronic object with a service life, and obsolescence is a genuine collecting problem for this medium.
patience: Not applicable -- far out of band.

analysis: Richard Lindner (NY/Germany, 1901-1978) at $1,000-1,500. A significant Pop-adjacent painter; at this price it will be a print.
problems: Out of band, just. Establish edition and signature.

analysis: Petrea Noyes (NY, 1946- ) at $6,000-8,000, the dearer of two.
problems: Far out of band, living artist.

analysis: The cheaper Petrea Noyes at $2,000-3,000.
problems: Out of band, living artist.

analysis: Hans Moller (PA/NY/Germany, 1905-2000) at $1,500-2,000. A German-American modernist with a modest but real market.
problems: Out of band.

analysis: Mersad Berber (Bosnia-Herzegovina, 1940-2012) at $1,000-2,000. A major Yugoslav printmaker and painter.
problems: Out of band. His market is in the Balkans and Vienna.

analysis: Bruno Lucchesi (NY, 1926-2016) at $1,000-1,500. An Italian-American figurative sculptor whose intimate bronzes sell steadily.
problems: Out of band, just. Lucchesi editioned his work, so establish the edition size and foundry. Five photographs.

analysis: Andy Warhol at $4,000-5,000. At that price this will be a print, a signed Interview cover, or a photograph rather than a major work.
problems: Far out of band. Warhol is also the most authentication-dependent name in modern art -- the Warhol Authentication Board's dissolution left the market reliant on provenance and stamped estate numbers. Three photographs and no medium stated.

analysis: David Schneuer (Israel/Germany, 1915-1988) at $2,000-3,000. A Weimar-era graphic designer turned painter with a following in Israel.
problems: Out of band. Schneuer is also heavily reproduced as prints and serigraphs; establish the medium.

analysis: James Coignard (France, 1925-2008) at $1,000-1,500. A French printmaker whose carborundum etchings were widely editioned.
problems: Out of band, just. Very large editions, so no scarcity.

analysis: Josef Wenzel Viktor Josephu (NY/Austria, 1889-1970) at $1,000-1,500. An Austrian-American sculptor working in the Deco idiom; career begins before 1926.
problems: Out of band, just. Note the catalogue misspells 'Viktkor'. Establish material and whether ivory elements are present, which would add the usual constraint.

analysis: John Bisbee (ME, 1965- ) at $3,500-5,500, with a second at 3291. Bisbee is a Brunswick, Maine sculptor who works exclusively in forged bright common nails -- a genuinely distinctive practice and a real Maine name, based fifteen minutes from Bath.
problems: Far out of band and a living artist with gallery representation. Only two photographs. Worth knowing as one of the strongest contemporary Maine names in the sale.

analysis: Georg Kolbe (Germany, 1877-1947) at $2,000-3,000. Kolbe was one of the major German figurative sculptors of the 20th century.
problems: Out of band. Kolbe's bronzes were cast posthumously in large numbers by the Kolbe Museum and others -- establish whether this is a lifetime cast, which is most of the value.

analysis: Marco Spalatin (NY/Croatia, 1945- ) at $2,000-3,000. A printmaker known for geometric serigraphs.
problems: Out of band, and a high estimate for editioned serigraphs by an artist with a modest record.

analysis: David Burliuk (1882-1967) at $1,000-1,500. Burliuk was the 'father of Russian Futurism' and a genuinely important figure in modernism who later settled on Long Island.
problems: Out of band, just. Burliuk is also among the most forged Russian-American painters -- he was prolific, his style is easy to imitate, and demand from Russian buyers has driven a large fake industry. Note the catalogue's odd punctuation, 'NY/UKRAINE - 1882-1967'.

analysis: Maria Bertran, contemporary California, at $3,000-4,000. A living plein-air painter working in a French Impressionist manner.
problems: Far out of band, wrong coast, living artist with an active gallery market.
